summary: Studies throughput limits for single-packet messages on the ARPANET, motivated by sending digitized speech, which needs high throughput for small messages. It finds that throughput degrades for such messages.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 632 explains how an out-of-order message can cause repeated retransmissions and lower throughput for single-packet traffic. It proposes two ways to accept later messages safely while preserving buffer space for messages that must arrive first.

subtitle: Why out-of-order single-packet messages could reduce ARPANET throughput.

tldr.problem: A test of high-rate single-packet traffic found much lower throughput than expected, a concern for applications such as digitized speech that need fast delivery of small messages.
tldr.mechanism: When a destination IMP receives a single-packet message out of order, it treats it as a buffer request and waits for the preceding message's RFNM; in RFNM-driven traffic, this can trigger repeated retransmissions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes two possible flow-control changes, but says the authors intended to pursue the issue with the IMP development group.

today: RFC 632 analyzes a throughput problem in ARPANET single-packet message flow control and describes possible changes for further discussion.

sections.title: The Single-Packet Throughput Test
sections.content:
The authors were studying small-message throughput for applications such as digitized speech. In a test sending single-packet messages from MOFFET to SRI, they expected more than 30 Kbps but observed less than 8 Kbps. They measured about 3.5 messages in transmission at once and channel utilization below 40%, while mean round-trip time was about 500 milliseconds.

The RFC says the unexpectedly low throughput was not explained by interfering traffic or channel utilization, so the authors examined the flow-control mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The test moved fewer small messages per second than expected even though the channels were not heavily used. The authors traced the problem to how the IMPs handled messages arriving out of order.

sections.title: How One Out-of-Order Message Delays Others
sections.content:
If a single-packet message arrives before its logical predecessor, the destination IMP does not accept it immediately. It treats it as a request for a reassembly buffer and sends an allocation only after processing the earlier message's RFNM. With RFNM-driven traffic, later messages may already have reached the destination IMP and be waiting for allocations.

The RFC's example shows that one out-of-order arrival can cause later messages to be retransmitted too, even if they arrived in order. Once this pattern starts, the authors say it may persist until the source stream is interrupted.
sections.plainLanguage: A message that arrives too early waits for its predecessor. In a fast stream, that delay can lead to repeated retransmissions of messages that follow it.

sections.title: Two Possible Flow-Control Changes
sections.content:
The first proposed change would reject an out-of-order single-packet message only while the buffer needs of earlier messages are unknown. Once those needs are known and buffers are set aside, later messages could be accepted safely; in the example, only one message needs retransmission.

The second proposal would accept or store all single-packet messages at first, then delete one if the destination IMP needs its buffer for an earlier message. Because the source IMP retains unacknowledged single-packet messages, the destination could later send an allocation for a deleted message. The authors say they planned to discuss these options with the IMP development group.
sections.plainLanguage: One option accepts out-of-order messages once earlier buffer needs are clear. Another stores them when possible and asks for retransmission only if a buffer is truly needed for an earlier message.
